messages.author: 5a5b99d05db5f9f4
messages.subject: adapting JAGS code to NIMBLE
parts:
Hi everyone,
I'm super new to NIMBLE coming from JAGS. I am used to ifelse statements in JAGS where I can assign a binary status to an indicator variable. I understand that ifelse statements do not work in NIMBLE and I tried to use a for loop with an if statement but I get errors. I have looked at past relevant answers but I'm not getting anywhere (example code below). Apologies if this is too basic. 

What is an alternative solution for ifelse statements in the context below:

for (i in 1:N){
  # Define latent state at first occasion
  z[i, f[i]] <- y[i, f[i]]  

  # Indicator variable with 0 or 1 if infection is absent or present
  Infection[i,f[i]] <- ifelse(z[i, f[i]] == 2, 1, 0)
}

Thanks! Andreas

messages.author: 73b37a8108370eea
messages.subject: Re: adapting JAGS code to NIMBLE
parts:
Hello Andreas,

A bit difficult to give you an option without knowing what the possible values of z are in your code. A bit more details about your code would help. If the only possible values of z are 1 and 2 you could simply put

Infection[i,f[i]] <- z[i,f[i]] - 1

Where all the 2s would become 1s and 1s would become 0s

 Otherwise, if the original state is known and not inferred, you could simply do that calculation outside of model code, put the first state of all your individuals in constants and feed that number to your infection variable inside model code. Something like: 

#Outside of model code, with your data being y:

initial.infection<-rep(NA, times=N)

for(i in 1:N){

initial.infection[i] <- ifelse(y[i,f[i]]==2,1,0)

}

my.constants<-list(

... all the constants...,

initial.infection)

 

Inside of model code:

for (i in 1:N){

  # Define latent state at first occasion
  z[i, f[i]] <- y[i, f[i]]  

  # Indicator variable with 0 or 1 if infection is absent or present

Infection[i,f[i]] <- initial.infection[i]

}

 (This also has the advantage of doing less calculations inside nimble code, which is always good to reduce memory use and can speed things up a bit.) 

Hope this helps! If this doesn't cut it you could provide a bit more details on your code or even better a reproducible example with fake data and it would make it easier to help.

Cheers,

Fred

messages.author: d78486bfff620d81
messages.subject: Re: adapting JAGS code to NIMBLE
parts:
Building on Fred's suggestion, one can also use arithmetic combined with `==` in cases like this.

For example, to make up a slightly more complicated case to illustrate -- suppose  `f[i]` could be 1 or 2 or 3, and 2 or 3 should become 1 and 1 should be come 0, 

Infection[i, f[i]] <- (z[i,f[i]]==2) + (z[i,f[i]] == 3)

And for complicated logic, one could write a nimbleFunction that takes z[i, f[i]] as the input argument and returns the desired result to be assigned to another model variable.

-Chris

parts:
Hi Andreas, if you define a nimbleFunction, it needs to be defined in R outside of the model. That appears to be the cause of the error message. So you'd first define `indicatorvarfstate` and then call `nimbleCode` to create the model code and then call `nimbleModel`. However, even after fixing that there would be some other issues with how you're setting things up.

But before we talk further about the nimbleFunction, if all that you are doing is setting infection to 1 if z[i,j] is 2, I think you can do this directly in the model code without needing the nimbleFunction

```

for (i in 1:N){
    # Define latent state at first occasion
    z[i, f.state[i]] <- y[i, f.state[i]]  
}

Infection[1:n, 1:m] <- z[1:n, 1:m] == 2
```

(For simplicity I've used `m` rather than dealing with the more complicated 2nd dimension of `y` in your code.)

If I've oversimplified things, I'm happy to discuss fixing up the nimbleFunction approach further.

messages.subject: Re: adapting JAGS code to NIMBLE
parts:
Hi Andreas, when used in a model, the `==` operator returns 1 or 0 depending on whether equality is found.

So if `z[1:n, 1:m]` equals 2, then `Infection[1:n, 1:m]` will be set to 1 and otherwise to 0.

Here's a simplified example:

```
> code <- nimbleCode({
+ infection <- z == 2
+ })
> m <- nimbleModel(code, inits = list(z = 2))

Building model
Setting data and initial values
Running calculate on model
  [Note] Any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables.
Checking model sizes and dimensions
> m$infection
[1] 1
```

Hi Andreas, if you define a nimbleFunction, it needs to be defined in R outside of the model. That appears to be the cause of the error message. So you'd first define `indicatorvarfstate` and then call `nimbleCode` to create the model code and then call `nimbleModel`. However, even after fixing that there would be some other issues with how you're setting things up.

But before we talk further about the nimbleFunction, if all that you are doing is setting infection to 1 if z[i,j] is 2, I think you can do this directly in the model code without needing the nimbleFunction

```
for (i in 1:N){
    # Define latent state at first occasion
    z[i, f.state[i]] <- y[i, f.state[i]]  
}
Infection[1:n, 1:m] <- z[1:n, 1:m] == 2
```

(For simplicity I've used `m` rather than dealing with the more complicated 2nd dimension of `y` in your code.)

If I've oversimplified things, I'm happy to discuss fixing up the nimbleFunction approach further.

Building on Fred's suggestion, one can also use arithmetic combined with `==` in cases like this.

For example, to make up a slightly more complicated case to illustrate -- suppose  `f[i]` could be 1 or 2 or 3, and 2 or 3 should become 1 and 1 should be come 0, 

Infection[i, f[i]] <- (z[i,f[i]]==2) + (z[i,f[i]] == 3)

And for complicated logic, one could write a nimbleFunction that takes z[i, f[i]] as the input argument and returns the desired result to be assigned to another model variable.

-Chris

On Wed, Jan 22, 2025 at 12:51 PM Frédéric LeTourneux <frederic....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello Andreas,

A bit difficult to give you an option without knowing what the possible values of z are in your code a bit more details about your code would help. 

If the only possible values of z are 1 and 2 you could simply put
Infection[i,f[i]] <- z[i,f[i]] - 1
Where all the 2s would become 1s and 1s would become 0s


Otherwise, if the original state is known and not inferred, you could simply do that calculation outside of model code, put the first state of all your individuals in constants and feed that number to your infection variable inside model code. Something like: 

#Outside of model code, with your data being y:
initial.infection<-rep(NA, times=N)
for(i in 1:N){
initial.infection[i] <- ifelse(y[i,f[i]]==2,1,0)
}
my.constants<-list(
... all the constants...,
initial.infection)

Inside of model code:
for (i in 1:N){
  # Define latent state at first occasion
  z[i, f[i]] <- y[i, f[i]]  

  # Indicator variable with 0 or 1 if infection is absent or present
  Infection[i,f[i]] <- initial.state[i]
}

Hope this helps! If this doesn't cut it you could provide a bit more details on your code or even better a reproducible example with fake data and it would make it easier to help.
Cheers,
